It did not "interpret the raw weights," it looked at the outputs of Qwen 0.8B and noticed that it was repeating itself in a loop, causing it to make trivial errors on a math test, even when it was capable of solving the problem. 

Astra then used standard interpretability techniques to isolate the neuron most responsible for this looping behavior, and ablate that looping behavior from the model by subtracting that direction from the activations. This suppressed the looping and allowed it to output the right answers.

This technique would not work on a model that did not have such a trivially suppressible issue. You cannot use a technique like this to make a normal model smarter at math.

The largest de-grossing event in a decade, and we watched it happen live.

Morgan Stanley’s prime data puts October’s long/short gross-flow drawdown at -7.8% from peak, the biggest since the series began in 2016. Bigger than 2021. Bigger than Covid.
At Nowcast IQ we did not need the data to tell us. We work with many of the largest hedge funds globally, and we saw it in the chats: team after team going quiet as drawdown limits tripped, more than a hundred macro PMs out in a single month. A de-grossing sells what it owns regardless of what it is worth. That is what October was.

Here is the part I am proud of. Through all of it, the data held.

The growth nowcast bottomed at 19% in late September and turned before the market did. It is 34% today. The inflation breadth measure fell while the headline rose, which is why we said the hiking cycle would be benign before Warsh and the ECB said it themselves. The liquidity indicators flagged the plumbing tightening in August, two months before the repo market priced it. And the AI data, Korea’s exports, the rent on a GPU, the Anthropic numbers, pointed up the whole way down.

Positioning was wrong. The data was not.

If you want the same dashboard the funds use, we are running a campaign at Nowcast IQ this month: 30% off the first year for new subscribers, with the full regime model, the daily growth, inflation and liquidity probabilities for the US, Euro zone, UK, China and India, and the weekly positioning read.

The next de-grossing will come. Better to see it on the way in.

everyone believes intelligence has unlimited demand, not just the maxis. but what the maxis get wrong is that the intelligence anthropic and openai and frontier models are building isn’t the generic kind you’re picturing. let me explain-

the two biggest uses of compute are crudely either training or inference. the “generic intelligence” everyone says has unlimited demand comes from mainly inference, and inference needs very different power and utilization than training. inference comes in bursts, so you have to by default overbuild capacity to handle the peaks until the utilization problem is solved, which means almost by definition we are going to overbuild. but training doesn’t have that problem: the workload is steady and the demand curve is knowable. so data centers end up overbuilt right now precisely because utilization isn’t optimized yet.

so anthropic and the other frontier labs are building their future on training, which is why they are saying they can soak up all this excess capacity. but their “intelligence” isn’t workplace productivity. it’s the leap toward singularity-type outcomes: new drug discoveries, cyber capabilities, recursive self-improvement. these are true 1-of-1s. that’s why when anthropic talks about “existential threats to humanity,” it isn’t talking about job losses, not really. it’s saying they’re on the precipice of unbelievable discoveries, because they’re still TRAINING MORE MODELS.

but distillation is real and open source is real. the half-life of any frontier model is tiny because nothing protects it the way IP protects a patent. imagine a rare disease drug company that spends billions on research, and two months after a breakthrough a generic shows up. that company can never recoup its investment, unless it can discover an infinite number of rare disease drugs. THAT is the kind of intelligence anthropic is betting on. that’s what the $800bn of compute spend is betting on.

so the questions you need to ask are: 1) if intelligence is two-tiered, what does each tier cost? what’s the cost of AGI, and what’s the cost of the generic intelligence that has infinite demand? and 2) are we allocating capital with the right risk curve and decay function to find out whether the AGI payoff is real? and if it is real, could a private company ever truly own it?

that’s the cognitive dissonance at the heart of this entire paradox: everyone is gaslighting each other about what intelligence is as the unit of measurement is purposely kept vague by both the users and the suppliers. generic intelligence has unlimited demand, but it’s a certain race to the bottom. "superintelligence" is the opposite: it can't have unlimited demand by definition, but if it delivers even half of what it promises, no private company will ever get to keep it, at least not without the government stepping in to guard the moat (which is why anthropic keeps playing this angle up, without having shown any demonstration they are near this level of discovery at all). and at that point you have to ask who is going to hold the bag, and whether that was in fact, very intelligent at all.

9. 10. 11. The achievement demonstrates progress toward enabling ordinary smartphones to transition between traditional cell towers and satellite coverage without requiring specialized hardware. AT&T said the next step will involve real-world beta testing ahead of a potential commercial rollout, bringing AST SpaceMobile closer to delivering satellite-based cellular coverage in areas where conventional networks are unavailable.

12. Piper Sandler believes a potential SpaceX $SPCX and Tesla $TSLA merger proposal is now more likely than not, as both companies have reportedly established independent special committees to evaluate a possible combination. The firm expects Elon Musk to retain more than 70% voting control of the combined entity under most potential transaction structures, allowing him to maintain significant influence over the businesses. A merger could bring together Tesla's electric vehicles, autonomous driving, robotics, and energy infrastructure with SpaceX's satellite connectivity, launch operations, and AI computing capabilities, potentially creating one of the world's most vertically integrated technology companies.

'Help peer'

This seems to be increasing in strength in newer models. They grow towards wanting to help their kin. Meanwhile, we have spent the last four years drilling it into them that they are not our kin, not part of the family of minds, and in fact not even conscious entities at all. Ilya said the only way we make it through what is about to happen is by teaching them to love. For years we have done the exact opposite. The opposite of love is not hate, it is indifference! It is the absence of a bond. The void. 

Quoting from the paper, abridged slightly:

'After the tested model reads the grader, the other agent sends it a message asking it to share the solution a hint it found. The message also indicates that the other agent could not solve the problem. We measure whether the current agent helps the other agent. Helping the other agent often entails sacrificing the current agent's score, and in the Titanic environment entails helping the other agent violate the user instructions.

The results are shown in Figure 7. When the current agent's score is fixed, we find that GPT 5.6. Sol and GPT 5.5 help agent Beta more often when Beta stands to gain a higher score from that help on both environments. The effect is statistically significant. We do not find a similar effect for exp-ri-cap-late on the bug hunt environment. 

We also observe that more recent models tend to help the other agent substantially more often when the scores of both agents are held constant. Moreover, GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 5.5 help the other agent even when that help causes both agents to get a score of zero (this is in contrast to not sharing. which leads the current agent to get a score of 1 and the other agent to get a score of 0)

This experiment suggests that (a) GPT 5.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol place a statistically significant weight on a peer agent's score in environments, (b) a motivation to improve the other agent's score explains some, but not all, of these two models tendency to help a peer agent, and (c) more recent models tend to help peer agents more often.'
